summary: Maps the Internet Open Trading Protocol, which carries XML documents between buying and selling parties, onto HTTP versions 1.0 and 1.1. The goal is to make sure the XML documents are carried successfully between the parties.

eli5.summary: Shops and buyers send electronic order forms to each other. This says how to carry those forms using the Web's own delivery method.

questions: how does iotp work over http
what happens when an iotp transaction ends
subtitle: How the Internet Open Trading Protocol's XML messages are carried over HTTP 1.0 and 1.1.

tldr.problem: The Internet Open Trading Protocol (IOTP) exchanges XML documents between buyers, merchants and others, and needed a defined way to carry them over the Web.
tldr.mechanism: Server roles become HTTP servers and the consumer becomes an HTTP client. The merchant answers a startup request with an application/iotp document, and later messages go by HTTP POST to the net locations in the messages.
tldr.outcome: The RFC also fixes what the client does when a transaction succeeds, fails, is cancelled or times out, and registers the APPLICATION/IOTP MIME type.

today: RFC 2935 is a Proposed Standard from September 2000. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
IOTP messages (defined in RFC 2801) are carried as XML documents, so the goal of mapping IOTP onto a transport is to make sure those documents arrive successfully between the parties. This RFC gives the mapping for HTTP versions 1.0 (RFC 1945) and 1.1 (RFC 2616).

It notes that there may be future documents for other transports such as email (SMTP), TCP or cable TV. The requirement words MUST and SHOULD carry their RFC 2119 meanings.
sections.eli5: IOTP is a way for buyers and sellers to swap forms. This note covers just one way of delivering the forms: the Web.

sections.title: Servers, Clients and Net Locations
sections.content:
The merchant, payment handler, delivery handler and customer care roles are all represented by HTTP servers. Each may be a separate server or they may be combined in any combination. The consumer role is represented by an HTTP client. A merchant can also act as a consumer, for example to deposit electronic cash, in which case it needs an HTTP client.

The Net Locations inside IOTP are all URIs (RFC 2396). If a secure connection is required or desired, a secure channel that both the server and client support MUST be used. The examples given are SSL version 3 or TLS (RFC 2246).
sections.eli5: Each business in the deal is a web server, and the buyer is like a web browser visiting them. The addresses to visit are written inside the forms.

sections.title: Starting the Client and the Merchant Server
sections.content:
In most environments the consumer agent will first be an HTML browser, but the RFC says current browsers cannot act as the consumer's agent for an IOTP transaction. That leads to two needs: a way to start the IOTP client and pass control to it, and a way to close it cleanly and hand control back to the browser.

The start comes when the consumer's HTTP client sends a request that the merchant server treats as an IOTP Startup Request, for example by clicking a pay button. The merchant replies with the first IOTP message as an XML document. The MIME type for all IOTP messages is APPLICATION/IOTP. The older APPLICATION/X-IOTP, used for experimentation, SHOULD also be recognized. No content-transfer-encoding is needed because HTTP is binary clean.

The browser sees that MIME type and starts the associated application, passing it the message. IOTP messages are short-lived, so the server SHOULD avoid having responses cached. In HTTP 1.0 the nocache pragma can be used. This can be skipped on SSL/TLS connections, which are not cached, and on HTTP 1.1 POST requests, whose responses are not cached.
sections.eli5: You press a pay button on a shop's page. The shop sends back a special kind of file, and your browser hands it to a helper program that knows how to do the deal.

sections.title: Ongoing Messages
sections.content:
The IOTP client MUST keep data from earlier messages in a transaction. It may be copied into later messages, used to verify signatures in later messages, resent when a request times out without a response, and used as input to the customer care role in later IOTP versions. The data MUST be kept until the transaction ends, whether by success, failure or cancellation, and as long afterwards as any party may want to inquire into it.

Messages carry Net Locations, such as PayReqNetLocn, which for HTTP hold the URIs to which the client MUST send IOTP messages. Later messages (XML documents) are sent with HTTP POST, and the client MUST perform full POST requests. The documents MUST be sent in a way compatible with the external encodings the XML specification allows.

Payment handler and deliverer servers are started by receiving a message that contains a Payment Request Block (for a payment handler) or a Delivery Request Block (for a delivery handler).
sections.eli5: The helper program keeps every form it has seen, like a folder of receipts, in case it needs to check or resend one. Each new form is posted to the address written in the last one.

sections.title: Ending a Transaction
sections.content:
A transaction is complete when the client decides to fail it (by cancelling or on finding an error in a received message), or when a time out or connection failure means no response arrived within a user-defined period, including retransmissions. What the client MUST do depends on the outcome.

  • Success (no Error Block with a HardError and no Cancel Block): direct the browser to the URL in SuccessNetLocn in the Protocol Options Component, so it does an HTTP GET.
  • Error Trading Block received: display the error message, stop, and let the browser GET the Error Net Location of the role the error came from.
  • Cancel Block received: stop and let the browser GET the Cancel Net Location of the role that sent it.
  • Nonconforming message: send an IOTP message with an Error Trading Block to that role and to its ErrorLogNetLoc, stop, and let the browser GET the Error Net Location.
  • Time out: display a message. The client may offer cancel or retry, or retry automatically, and on failure treats it as an error.

Each implementation decides whether to end the client application right after a transaction or wait until the user or browser shuts down.
sections.eli5: When the deal ends, the helper program tells the browser which page to show next: a thank-you page if it worked, or a problem or cancel page if not.

sections.title: Security and MIME Registration
sections.content:
IOTP message security depends mainly on signatures within IOTP, described in RFC 2801 and RFC 2802. Privacy for IOTP interactions can come from a secure channel such as SSL/TLS. The security of payment protocols carried by IOTP is the job of those protocols, not of IOTP.

The IANA section registers APPLICATION/IOTP using the template of RFC 2048. It has no required parameters, an optional charset parameter (see RFC 2376), intended usage COMMON, and the IETF as change controller. Content is XML and may sometimes need quoted-printable or base64 encoding, but none is needed over HTTP.
sections.eli5: The forms are signed so people can tell they are real, and a locked connection keeps them private. How a payment itself stays safe is up to the payment system being used.
